issues.body: The rejection loop covers inf, infinity, Infinity, INFINITY, nan, NAN but not the signed spellings Rust also accepts (e.g. '-Infinity', '+inf', '-nan'). The new whitelist does reject them (I verified old("-Infinity")=Some(-inf) vs new("-Infinity")=None), so this is only a gap in regression coverage, not in behaviour — a future refactor that re-loosened the predicate for signs would not be caught by this test.
issues.fix_hint: Add "-Infinity", "+inf", "-nan" to the first array in parse_xsd_float_rejects_non_xsd_rust_spellings.
issues.title: Rejection list omits '-Infinity' / '+inf', the signed Rust spellings

issues.body: The second loop checks parse_xsd_float(lex).is_some() for INF/+INF/-INF/NaN/1/-1.5/2E+3 but never checks the value, so a predicate change that made every accepted lexical parse to the wrong magnitude (or that swapped +INF/-INF) would still pass. The values are already covered indirectly by value_equality_across_lexical_forms, so this is low-value hardening.
issues.fix_hint: Assert concrete values for the finite cases, e.g. assert_eq!(parse_xsd_float("2E+3"), Some(2000.0)) and assert_eq!(parse_xsd_float("-INF"), Some(f64::NEG_INFINITY)), keeping is_some() only for the NaN case.
issues.title: Acceptance half of the test asserts only is_some(), not the parsed value

verdict.summary: Replaces the old blacklist in parse_xsd_float (reject 'x'/'X', trailing f/F/d/D, substring "inf") with a whitelist of the only bytes that can occur in an XSD float/double numeric lexical form ([0-9], '+', '-', '.', 'e', 'E'), keeping the special values INF/+INF/-INF/NaN in the preceding match arms. This is a real soundness fix, not a cosmetic one: Rust's f64 FromStr is case-insensitive for inf/infinity/nan, so the old case-sensitive `contains("inf")` blacklist let 'Infinity', 'INFINITY', '-Infinity', 'nan' and 'NAN' through as valid xsd:float/xsd:double values. I confirmed that empirically by compiling both the old and new predicates side by side: old("Infinity")=Some(inf), old("nan")=Some(NaN), while new(...)=None for both; all legal forms ('1', '.5', '1.', '1e5', '2E+3', '+INF', '1e10000') are unchanged. The whitelist is a correct characterisation of the lexical space rather than a heuristic: Rust's Number grammar (Digit+ | Digit+ '.' Digit* | Digit* '.' Digit+, optional ('e'|'E') Sign? Digit+) and XSD's noDecimalPtNumeral/decimalPtNumeral/scientificNotationNumeral coincide exactly once the alphabet is restricted to those bytes, so there is neither over-acceptance nor under-acceptance, and non-ASCII bytes and whitespace-padded lexicals are rejected too. Empty string still falls through to a failing parse. Both callers are the xsd:float and xsd:double arms of xsd_value (entail.rs:398,403); no other call sites exist, so the stricter behaviour is confined to D-entailment value mapping, where an ill-formed float correctly becomes an inconsistency. The new unit test is non-vacuous: 4 of its 6 rejection cases (Infinity, INFINITY, nan, NAN) returned Some under the pre-diff code, so it goes red on revert, and it pins both parse_xsd_float and the xsd_value float/double surface. cargo test -p sparq-conformance --lib inference::entail passes (5/5). Only nits remain.
